question.:question/problem: Given the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}$, find a basis of $\text{Null}(A).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $A$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 & 1 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 & -1 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation $Ax=0$ is equivalent to the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{4} &=0 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{4} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The general solution is ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{4}$ and ${x}_{2}=-{x}_{3}-{x}_{4},$ where ${x}_{3}$ and ${x}_{4}$  are  free variables. Therefore, if $x\in \text{Null}(A),$ then

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-{x}_{4} \\ -{x}_{3}-{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{4}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3},\,{x}_{4}\in R.
$$

This implies that 

$$
B=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\right\}
$$

is a basis of $\text{Null}(A)$ since it is a linearly independent set and its vectors generate $\text{Null}(A).$

question.:question/problem:
For the vector $u=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $u⊥W,\,$ where  $$
\displaystyle W=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3} \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\right\}
$$

II. $u⊥H,\,$ where  $$
\displaystyle H=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\right\}
$$

III. $u⊥V,\,$ where  $V=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\right\}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $W,H$ and $V$ as $\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2}\},\{{h}_{1},{h}_{2},{h}_{3}\}$ and  $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$, respectively.   

Now, we have to compute the dot product between $u$ and the vectors in each set. 

- For the set $W:$

$$
u\cdot {w}_{1}=3\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)+1\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1=-1\ne 0\,\times
$$

So, $u⊥̸W.$ Notice that we stopped after finding the first non-orthogonal vector in the set.

- For the set $H:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {h}_{1} & =3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1=0\,✓ \\ u\cdot {h}_{2} & =3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 0+1\cdot (-1)=-4\ne 0\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $u⊥̸H.$ Notice that we stopped after finding the first non-orthogonal vector in the set.

- For the set $V:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {v}_{1} & =3\cdot \frac{2}{3}+1\cdot (-1)+1\cdot (-1)=0\,✓ \\ u\cdot {v}_{2} & =3\cdot 0+1\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1=0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $u⊥V.$

Hence, the correct answer is "III only".

The equation of the line using the cross product takes the general form

$$
(r-p)\times v=0,
$$

where $v$ is the direction vector of the line and $p$ is the position vector of a point that lies in the line.

From the equation of our line with cross product, we obtain that its vector equation is 

$$
r=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the image of the line $r=p+tv$ under the action of $T$, we need to compute the images of $p$ and $v$ under the action of $T:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(p) & =T\,p \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 11 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ T(v) & =T\,v \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-20 \\ 5 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the image is $r=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 11 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-20 \\ 5 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$

question.:question/problem:
Find $\text{rank}(A)$ given that $$
\displaystyle \text{Null}(A)=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,|\,\,{x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R\right\}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
According to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A)=n.
$$

For the given matrix, we have $n=5,$ since this is the number of components in each of the vectors of the null space. 

Also, since 

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\left\{{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,|\,\,{x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R\right\}
$$

we conclude that $\text{nullity}(A)=2.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ \text{rank}(A)+2 & =5 \\ \text{rank}(A) & =5-2 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\left\{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\right\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\left\{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\right\}$

III. $\left\{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\right\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}=-2\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}+2\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ can't be written as a linear combination of 

$$
\left\{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\right\}
$$

since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{11}=-{a}_{12}:$

$$
a\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}+b\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ -b & -a\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

question.:question/problem:
Consider the linear transformation $$
\displaystyle T:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}3x-9y+3z \\ 2x-5y+2z \\ 6x-4y+6z\end{bmatrix}.

question.:question/worked-solution:
Finding the kernel of $T$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $T.$

Fror the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -9 & 3 \\ 2 & -5 & 2 \\ 6 & -4 & 6\end{bmatrix}.$

Setting $x=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix},$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we find reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -9 & 3 \\ 2 & -5 & 2 \\ 6 & -11 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & -9 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 6 & -11 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & -9 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-7{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & -9 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$ and $y$, and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $y.$

From the second equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting these into the first equation, we have $x=-z.$ 

Therefore, the kernel of the linear transformation $\,T$ is $\left\{\begin{bmatrix}-z \\ 0 \\ z\end{bmatrix}\,:\,z\in R\right\}.$

$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}^{T}\cdot {\left(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 10 \\ 20\end{bmatrix}$, we get

$$

$$

$$

What is the value of $\,a+b+c,\,$ given that  

$$
T({b}_{1})=\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,T({b}_{2})=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{bmatrix},\,T({b}_{3})=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}.$ The $B$-matrix for $T$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B.$

To find the coordinates of $T({b}_{1}),$ $T({b}_{2}),$ and $T({b}_{3})$ relative to the basis $B$, we consider the matrix

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}| & | & | & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) & T({b}_{3}) \\ | & | & | & | & | & |\end{array}\right].
$$

Now, we reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination. Then, on the right-hand side, we will obtain the $B$-matrix for $T:$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}0 & 0 & 4 & 8 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1 & 1 & 0 & 2 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 8 & 4 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}: &=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1 & 1 & 0 & 2 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}: &={R}_{2}-2{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1 & 1 & 0 & 2 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -5 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}: &={R}_{1}-{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1 & 0 & 0 & 7 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -5 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
[\,T\,]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}7 & -1 & -3 \\ -5 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, $a=2,$ $b=-2,$ $c=-3$ and 

$$
a+b+c=2+(-2)+(-3)=-3.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}

{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,B=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}| \\ {v}_{1} \\ |\end{bmatrix}\,,\begin{bmatrix}| \\ {v}_{2} \\ |\end{bmatrix}\,,\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}\right\}
$$

Suppose that $V=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$ Given that $B$ is an orthogonal basis for $V,$ and that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We find an orthogonal basis $B$ of $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows:

**Step 1.** We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2.** We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the usual formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\left(2\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** We find the vector ${v}_{3}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ using the usual formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\frac{\left(\frac{9}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{9}{2}\right)}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\left(2\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\right) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=0,$ $c=2,$ and $\frac{a}{c}=\frac{0}{2}=0.$

question.:question/problem:
Find the value of ${x}_{4}-{x}_{1}$ given that  $6a-2x=b$ and

$$
a=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 6 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ 10 \\ 48 \\ -10\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6a-2x & =b \\ -2x & =b-6a \\ x & =-\frac{1}{2}(b-6a) \\ x & =-\frac{1}{2}\left(\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ 10 \\ 48 \\ -10\end{bmatrix}-6\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 6 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}\right) \\ x & =-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4 \\ 12 \\ 14\end{bmatrix} \\ x & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ -6 \\ -7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{4}-{x}_{1}=-7-1=-8.$

question.:question/problem:
Find the value of ${x}_{2}+{x}_{3}$ given that $3a-5x=b$ and

$$
a=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ 5 \\ 17\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3a-5x & =b \\ -5x & =b-3a \\ x & =-\frac{1}{5}(b-3a) \\ x & =-\frac{1}{5}\left(\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ 5 \\ 17\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\right) \\ x & =-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}15 \\ -10 \\ 20\end{bmatrix} \\ x & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=2-4=-2.$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true, given that $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $$
\text{Null}(A)=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}-4{x}_{1} \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 3{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}\mid {x}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}\right\}?
$$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$$ A\text{ is invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\left\{\begin{aligned}\text{Col}(A)&=\mathbb{R}^{4} \\ \text{rank}(A)&=4 \\ \text{Null}(A)&=\{0\} \\ \text{nullity}(A)&=0\end{aligned}\right. $$

The supplied nullspace can be written as the span of the independent vectors in

$${x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}$$

Hence $\text{dim(Null}(A))=1$, so $A$ is not invertible.

We have $\text{rank}(A)<4$, $\text{nullity}(A)>0$, $\text{Null}(A)\ne\{0\}$, and $\text{Col}(A)\ne\mathbb{R}^{4}$. In particular, $\text{rank}(A)=3$ and $\text{nullity}(A)=1$.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement $\text{dim(Null}(A))=1$ is true. $\text{nullity}(A)=1$.

- Statement $A\text{ is invertible}$ is false. $A$ is not invertible.

- Statement $\text{rank}(A)\ne 4$ is true. $\text{rank}(A)=3$; the rank counts pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{dim(Null}(A))=1$; $\text{rank}(A)\ne 4$ only.
